summary: A linked list stores values in separate nodes, each pointing to the next one. Adding at the front is O(1), but reaching index i takes i steps.
notes: for (let current = this.head; current !== null; current = current.next) is the standard traversal loop.
insertAt sets newNode.next before current.next. Reversing those two lines loses the rest of the list.
A template literal like `Playlist: ${playlist}` calls toString(). console.log(playlist) would print the nested node objects instead.
pitfall: Calling insertAt with an index past the end makes current become null, and current.next throws TypeError: Cannot read properties of null (reading 'next').
contrast: JavaScript ends the list with null like Java, but its Node class has no types, so like Python's, next could hold anything. JavaScript also has undefined, and a missing next set to undefined would not stop a loop that checks !== null.
